title: Puberty ritual turns ordeal for Wayanad tribal girls; one forced to spend 40 days in bamboo enclosure
content: Kalpetta: A Class 8 tribal girl in Wayanad was allegedly forced to spend nearly 40 days in a makeshift enclosure of bamboo poles and tarpaulin sheets, isolated from her family and the outside world. Reason: She attained puberty. The customary post-puberty ritual required her family to organise a feast for members of the settlement. Unable to raise the estimated 20,000 needed for the ceremony, her father insisted that she remain in the enclosure until the rituals were completed. The bizarre ordeal was faced by a girl belonging to the Kattunaikka tribal community in Wayanad. Her nightmare began when she attained puberty towards the end of September. She was finally allowed to return to school only in the first week of November, after teachers, local representatives and officials intervened to help her family organise the customary feast. Till then, for nearly 40 days, the young girl endured extreme weather conditions, exposed to the scorching sun, rain and cold, inside a cramped enclosure barely two-and-a-half feet wide. The makeshift structure, locally known as a 'kommakoodu' (a nest-like structure), was set up near the family home in an area frequented by wild animals, particularly at night. The isolation meant that the Class 8 student had to stay away from her studies, classmates and the familiar surroundings of home at a crucial stage of her childhood. Teachers step in The prolonged absence of the girl from school eventually alerted her teachers at Government Higher Secondary School, Cheeral, who began making enquiries and reaching out to the family and community members. They then visited her. A teacher from her former school, Government UP School, Kallinkara, near Sulthan Bathery, also highlighted the issue at a meeting of teachers. The matter subsequently reached the police, officials of Tribal Development, Health and local body representatives, who visited the girl and assured the family of support. However, her father remained adamant that she could return home and resume school only after the customary feast was conducted. Cheeral school principal Nisha KR, and the headmaster of her former school, Benoy, along with Parents' Teachers' Association (PTA) office bearers, other teachers and local representatives, offered to arrange provisions, vegetables and other essentials required for the feast. However, the cost of liquor, considered an essential component of the ritual to appease the community's traditional deities and chieftains, emerged as the final hurdle. "Finally, we decided to mobilise funds to rescue the girl from this uncertain ordeal," said Preethy Surendran, ward member of Nenmeni grama panchayat. An intervention by the office of Wayanad MP Priyanka Gandhi and IC Balakrishnan MLA helped. "Local representatives and others also contributed towards conducting the customary rituals and feast," said Preethy Surendran, adding that the practice of isolating girls following puberty was prevalent in the Kattunaikka tribe's settlements. A family caught between tradition and hardship The family's circumstances made the situation even more complicated. The girl's mother had left the family, leaving the father to look after their three daughters. A daily-wage agricultural labourer, he was struggling financially and was under considerable mental stress. "Though we did everything possible to secure the girl's release from the enclosure, the family's situation was extremely difficult," said Baby Cheeral, a Block Panchayat member. The local representatives were also concerned that any coercive intervention could trigger social ostracism of the family within the community and possibly lead to an adverse reaction from the distressed father. "We were more worried about the consequences of forcibly shifting the girl to a government-run institution with the help of the police and health workers...
